title: I'll say it myself (1916)
hookLine: Henrietta Szold thanked a friend who offered to say Kaddish for her mother, and said she would say it herself
tomorrow: what did a young student forget at sunset in Berlin?

cards: Noa sent the application last night. This morning her mom offered to be the one to tell Saba David she might be gone the summer he settles into his new place. Noa typed back: thanks, i'll tell him myself.
Someone answered almost those words long ago. Henrietta Szold, a writer, teacher and the founder of Hadassah, lost her mother. Kaddish, the mourner's prayer, was traditionally said by sons.
Her mother had none. A kind friend, Haym Peretz, offered to say it for them.

teach.b: Her reply is a letter, and it starts with gratitude. She tells him his offer moved her deeply. Then she says no, and explains.
As she understood it, a child says Kaddish to take up the parent's bond with the Jewish people and carry it on.
Her mother had daughters, and Szold believed that bond was now hers to carry, not something to hand to anyone, however loving.
Women had been freed from some duties, she wrote, but she didn't read that as a door shut when they can do the work themselves. So she said it herself, in her own voice, for her own mother.
Communities still answer this differently: in some, traditionally only men say Kaddish aloud; in others, women say it too.
What the letter shows is how to decline a gift without dropping it: thank the giver, then pick up the weight.

how: Mourners say Kaddish, a prayer praising God, with a minyan during the mourning period and on the anniversary of a death; communities differ on whether women say it aloud.

games.q: what does “i'll say it myself” mean?
o: repeating your own words aloud so you remember them
insisting on doing everything alone, without help
taking on a duty in your own voice instead of handing it off

games.q: a week of later voices — tap the pairs.
p: meet the you; hallow the everyday
not yet; from life to text
thanked her friend, said Kaddish herself

s: Szold turned down her friend's offer coldly
her letter starts by thanking him and saying how much it moved her.
Szold saw Kaddish as a child carrying on a parent's bond
that's why she believed it was hers to say.
every Jewish community has the same practice on women and Kaddish

games.q: your cousin offers to give the toast at your dad's retirement because you hate public speaking. what would Szold's letter suggest?
o: thank him warmly, then give it yourself, short and true.
let him do it; what matters is that it's said well.
skip the toast; love doesn't need a speech.
games.why: Szold thanked her friend first, then said Kaddish herself: the bond was hers to carry.

practice: Find a pen. Write one responsibility you'll carry yourself instead of handing it off: a call, a visit, a hard sentence to someone you love. Sign it with your first name, and keep the paper where you'll see it.

wordCard.voice: I'll say it myself: Henrietta Szold's answer to a friend's kind offer, thanking him and saying Kaddish for her mother in her own voice.

orig.note: Aramaic: holy. the mourner's prayer, which praises God.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: I'll say it myself. Thank the giver first, then lift what's yours, and the week's six lines come back as a game.
